memory_update.text: Core direct AI networking universe for this node should include NVDA, AVGO, ANET, MRVL, and CRDO as first-pass US-listed candidates.

The node splits into at least five investable sublayers: full-stack AI fabrics, Ethernet switch systems, merchant switch/NIC silicon, optical/electrical DSP and SerDes, and short-reach cable/interconnect components.

Optical module makers and photonics suppliers such as Coherent, Lumentum, Fabrinet, and potential smaller photonics names were not included due to the five-candidate cap but should be covered in a dedicated optics pass.

Cisco was not included in the top five because its AI networking exposure is diluted by broader enterprise and security businesses, but Cisco Silicon One, Nexus, and AI PODs warrant follow-up as a diversified incumbent.

Astera Labs was not included due to the five-candidate cap, but its PCIe/CXL retimers, Ethernet smart cable modules, and fabric switches make it relevant for a separate intra-rack connectivity screen.
Add MRVL as a core AI interconnect silicon candidate: optical DSPs, SerDes, switches, custom silicon, active cable DSPs, and CPO architecture.
Add COHR and LITE as optical-component and laser bottleneck candidates; prioritize verification of InP/EML capacity, 800G/1.6T revenue, and hyperscaler design wins.
Add CRDO as a focused in-rack AI connectivity candidate through active electrical cables and SerDes products linking GPUs and switches.
Add APH as a broad physical-interconnect supplier with documented AI-related IT datacom strength and expanded fiber/cable capabilities via acquisition.

Potential next-pass candidates not included due to 5-name cap: GLW for optical fiber and AI datacenter connectivity; FN as optical manufacturing/packaging partner; CIEN for data-center interconnect and 800G/1.6T coherent pluggables; AAOI for smaller-cap 800G/1.6T transceivers; SMTC/MTSI for optical and high-speed analog components.
Add MRVL, CRDO, ALAB, FN, and COHR as priority US-listed candidates for the AI networking and optical-interconnect node.

The node should be split into sublayers for future passes: switch/NIC silicon, AEC/copper short-reach, optical DSPs, optical transceiver/component suppliers, optical manufacturing services, and fabric observability/software.

LITE, CIEN, APH, TEL, MTSI, ONDS/POET-class smaller photonics names, and private/foreign optical module suppliers were not fully expanded in this five-name pass and should be covered in a dedicated optics/components pass.

Customer mapping remains incomplete: hyperscaler design wins, customer concentration, and whether revenue is tied to AI training clusters, inference clusters, telecom, or general datacenter refresh need primary-source confirmation.

summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the directly exposed US-listed universe for the AI networking and optical/interconnect node. The highest-confidence candidates are full-stack AI fabric owners, Ethernet/InfiniBand switch and NIC silicon leaders, data-center switching platforms, and high-speed interconnect component suppliers. This pass intentionally prioritizes direct exposure over broader AI semiconductor or cloud demand exposure. Expanded the AI networking/optical-interconnect universe beyond seed names toward suppliers tied to potential chokepoints: optical DSPs, 800G/1.6T optics, InP/EML lasers, active electrical cables, high-speed connectors, and fiber-optic interconnect systems. The highest-relevance additions are Marvell for AI interconnect silicon and DSPs; Coherent and Lumentum for lasers/optical components; Credo for AEC/DSP connectivity inside AI racks; and Amphenol for high-speed copper/fiber interconnect infrastructure. This is a research universe expansion only, not a recommendation. Expanded the US-listed universe for the AI networking and optical-interconnect node beyond the seed list. The most relevant second-order mappings are: high-speed DSP/SerDes and custom interconnect silicon, AEC copper interconnects, PCIe/CXL/Ethernet retimers and smart fabric modules, optical transceiver/component suppliers, and outsourced optical-manufacturing capacity.
